story:
One of this beech's branches grew so long that it put down roots of its own in the flower bed beyond the path. The Friends of the Public Garden, who care for the Garden's trees alongside the city, described it in 2019 as a venerable specimen reaching out over the walkway and over the Bagheera fountain, with that rooted limb cabled back to its many-stemmed trunk to keep the whole thing together.

The Garden holds fourteen beeches, and the Friends say some of them date from its original plantings in the 1870s. Of this one they wrote that it may be over 150 years old, which is an estimate, not a planting record. It is by far the biggest beech in the Garden. The city's tree inventory gives its stems a combined 71 inches across, where the next largest beech is 60.

Age has a cost. In the same 2019 note the Friends reported that the tree was in decline, with significant rot inside, and that they were working to prolong its life, possibly by taking weight off the crown. No public word on its health has followed since. The city inventory still lists it, and that is the latest record we have. If you visit and it has changed, tell us.

It stands on the Lagoon Path, over the fountain with the panther, a few minutes' walk from Arlington station.

story:
Only one Japanese pagoda tree in Massachusetts is bigger than this one. The state's register measured it in January 2023 at 196 inches round, almost five metres, and 72 feet tall, and ranked it second of its kind in the Commonwealth. The city's own inventory of Public Garden trees agrees on the trunk, and has no other pagoda tree in the Garden anywhere near its size.

The tree does its best work late in the year. Pagoda trees flower in late summer, sending out sprays of cream blossom in August, when almost nothing else in bloom is a tree. On the Arlington Street side, this broad, spreading crown becomes one of the few things in flower overhead.

The Garden's west side keeps good company. The dawn redwood planted here in 1963 stands about 45 metres away, and a short walk takes in the Garden's biggest ginkgo and its biggest bur oak, all three within about 40 metres of each other. Three of the Garden's biggest trees in one corner, and it costs nothing to walk through.

Nobody has published a planting date for the pagoda tree. Its trunk is thick and deeply fissured, which tells you it is old without telling you how old. If you know, tell us.

best_time.label: August, when sprays of cream flowers open and almost no other tree is in bloom

story:
Among the roughly 1,500 trees the city has recorded on Boston Common, in the Public Garden and along the Commonwealth Avenue Mall, there is exactly one rock elm, and it stands near the Public Garden's tool shed. The Friends of the Public Garden call it the lone specimen of its species in all three parks, and the city's inventory agrees.

Rock elm is a North American tree that is rare in cultivation, even in North America. Harvard's Arnold Arboretum titled an article on it "the hard elm that's hard to find", and the title holds up. Seeing one in the middle of a city park is the exception, not the rule, and this one has no relatives nearby to give it away.

This one is a good size, 36 inches across in the city's records, about 2.9 metres round. That is not huge by the standards of the Garden's beeches and oaks, and it does not need to be. Its distinction is the species, not the girth. Walk past it without knowing and it reads as one more elm among the hundreds in these parks.

Nobody has published when it was planted, or why a gardener chose a rock elm for the Public Garden in the first place. If you know either part of that story, tell us. The Bagheera beech and the Garden's lagoon are a short walk away.

story:
Boston Common is full of elms and, according to the people who look after them, has exactly one true American elm left. The Friends of the Public Garden describe it as the last true, non-hybridized American elm on the Common, standing on Railroad Mall just west of the Visitor Information Center.

That matters because of what happened to the rest. American elm is the state tree of Massachusetts, and before Dutch elm disease the three downtown parks held thousands of elms. The Friends now count just over 400 elms across the Common, the Garden and the Commonwealth Avenue Mall, about a quarter of all their trees.

The city's tree inventory backs up the Friends' claim in its own way. It lists other trees on the Common as American elm, but none larger than 23 inches across. This one is 46, about 3.7 metres round, which puts it in a different class from anything else of its kind on the Common.

Nobody has published an age for it, and no planting date survives in the records. If you know it, tell us. The best view is from the Mall itself, looking up into the vase of branches, the shape that lets you pick an American elm out from the English elms around it. It has outlived thousands of elms in these parks, which is reason enough to stop.

story:
The only white oak in Franklin Square stands among rows of littleleaf lindens, and Massachusetts ranks it eighteenth of its species in the whole state. The register measured it in March 2021 at 135.5 inches round, about 3.4 metres, and 68 feet tall. The city's later inventory has the trunk a little wider still, at 45 inches across.

Eighteenth sounds modest, but the list covers the whole Commonwealth, and this tree earned its place in a city square in the South End, on Washington Street, with houses on every side.

Boston's best-known white oak, on Peters Hill in the Arnold Arboretum, has been core-sampled and dated to the early 1800s. This one has never been dated, and nothing published gives a planting year. Its girth makes it a mature tree, but girth alone does not give an honest age for an oak in a city square. If you know when it went in, tell us.

Franklin Square has one more big tree worth a look on the same visit, an American elm about 55 inches across that is not on the state list.

story:
For most of the year this is a big tree in a garden full of big trees. For a day or two in November it is the one everybody stops for. Ginkgos turn butter gold all at once, then let go of nearly every leaf in a single drop, and a crown this size leaves a carpet of yellow fans across the lawn on the Garden's west side.

It is the largest ginkgo the city has recorded in the Public Garden and on Boston Common, 53.8 inches across, about 4.3 metres round, against 39.4 for the next one down. That figure comes from the city's tree inventory alone. No register or published account gives this tree's size or history, so treat the measurement as one good source rather than a settled fact.

Ginkgo has been planted in these parks for a long time, and the Friends of the Public Garden have written about the species in these parks. None of that writing dates this particular tree, and neither does anything else published. If you know when it went in, tell us.

It stands a few metres from the Garden's biggest bur oak and about 45 metres from the state's second-largest pagoda tree, so one short loop on the Arlington Street side covers all three. Come in November for the gold, or in August, when the pagoda tree is in flower and the ginkgo is a plain green giant beside it.

best_time.label: November, when the whole crown turns butter gold and drops in a day or two

story:
Macrocarpa means big fruit, and this oak's acorns sit in cups edged with a shaggy fringe. It is the broadest of the Public Garden's six bur oaks, 53.1 inches across in the city's tree inventory, about 4.2 metres round. The next one down is 41.4.

That inventory is the only record of this tree's size. No register lists it and nothing published gives its history, so the figure stands on one good source. It is still a big oak by any standard for a city garden, and it has a lot of company. The Garden's biggest ginkgo stands about ten metres away and the state's second-largest Japanese pagoda tree a little further on, so this corner of the Arlington Street side packs three of the Garden's largest trees into a space you can cross in a minute.

Bur oak is a North American species, and its big, deeply lobed leaves are almost as distinctive as the acorns, which come down under the crown in autumn.

Nobody has published when this tree was planted, and its girth alone is not an honest guide to the age of an oak in a city garden. If you know its story, tell us. It is a three-minute walk from Arlington station.

story:
Fourth place in Massachusetts for swamp white oak belongs to a tree beside the tennis courts at Dilboy Field, in West Somerville. The state measured it in December 2019 at 171 inches round, about 4.34 metres, and only 54.6 feet tall. For a tree that wide, that is short, and it gives the oak a squat, heavy build.

The Latin name, bicolor, describes the leaves, which are green on top and silvery underneath. It is the easiest way to tell it from other oaks nearby.

Dilboy Field is a public memorial park on the Alewife Brook Parkway, and the register places the tree at its tennis courts without giving a closer position. The pin on this page marks the park, not the trunk, so walk the edge of the courts and look for the widest oak you can find.

The state's measurement is nearly seven years old and the register does not record the tree's condition. The most recent sign of it is a 2023 nature-app record from within the park, which may or may not be this tree. So treat this one as a tree to confirm. If you visit, tell us whether it still stands and send a photograph, which would settle both the pin and the question. Nobody has dated it either, so any history you know is welcome too.
